science.title: Quantum computing-enhanced deep learning for real-time detection and mitigation of cyberattack patterns
science.description: Cyberattacks are increasing in sophistication. As a result, traditional cybersecurity systems based on classical computing and conventional deep-learning techniques are increasingly exhibiting limitations and vulnerabilities. Although deep-learning models offer substantial advantages over traditional methods for automated intrusion detection through large-scale security data analysis and pattern recognition, they suffer from notable constraints related to high-dimensional feature spaces, scalability, and stringent real-time inference requirements. This work proposes a quantum-enhanced deep learning (QEDL) framework for detecting and mitigating real-time cyberattack patterns. Quantum computing technologies—specifically quantum feature selection and quantum data encoding—are integrated into a classical–hybrid quantum deep-learning architecture. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is employed for quantum feature selection to enable efficient identification of discriminative features from high-dimensional cybersecurity datasets. In addition, quantum data encoding exploits superposition and entanglement to process multiple complex inputs simultaneously. The resulting quantum feature representations are processed using parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), followed by classical deep-learning layers for accurate threat classification. The proposed QEDL framework is evaluated using the CIC–IDS2017 dataset, and its performance is compared against classical deep-learning models and pure quantum neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that, within the proposed hybrid quantum–classical framework, the QAOA-based feature selection strategy achieved higher classification performance than the evaluated classical feature selection methods under the reported experimental settings. In addition, the proposed framework exhibited improved generalization to previously unseen attacks. These findings suggest that the proposed hybrid quantum–classical framework is a promising approach for cyberattack detection under the experimental conditions considered in this study. The experiments in this study were simulated using IBM Aer backend, without physical quantum hardware. The results obtained in this study serve as a simulation-based proof of concept.

science.title: Sensory plasticity of dorsal horn silent neurons as a critical mechanism for neuropathic pain
science.description: The spinal cord dorsal horn (DH) integrates sensory processing but undergoes critical plasticity following nerve injury, leading to mechanical allodynia, or “touch-evoked pain”. It has been proposed that after nerve injury, innocuous sensory neurons gain access to nociceptive-specific (NS) circuits in the DH due to altered spinal inhibitory controls, thereby converting touch into pain. It is however unclear how sensory processing is reorganized under these conditions to generate this symptom. In this study, we used two-photon calcium imaging in mice to show that spinal disinhibition or nerve injury converts most DH excitatory neurons into highly polymodal cells, and unmasks an unprecedented number of previously silent neurons responding to a wide dynamic range (WDR) of sensory modalities. Using computational modeling, we further show that neuropathic pain likely does not result primarily from the transformation of excitatory NS neurons into WDR neurons, but rather from the activation of this previously dormant circuit. Nerve injury alters sensory processing leading to neuropathic pain. In this study, the authors show that loss of spinal inhibition after injury in mice does not seem to let nociceptive neurons be activated by innocuous stimuli, but rather unmasks a previously silent circuit which likely drives pain.

science.title: Longer nights bring more chances to see northern lights
science.description: As the nights get longer and darker, Moose Jaw-area skywatchers will have more opportunities to catch a glimpse of the aurora borealis. Abigail Sadowski, resident astronomer at Kalium Observatory, said the northern lights can be unpredictable, but there are resources that can help people know when conditions are favourable. “We did recently have some really good ones that I could even see while I was in Cypress Hills about a week or two ago,” Sadowski said. The aurora is caused by charged particles interacting with Earth’s magnetic field and upper atmosphere. When geomagnetic activity increases, Sadowski said, the auroral oval can expand farther south, making the northern lights visible to more people.
